title: Lighting & Materials
description: Light 3D surfaces with normals, shading, shadows, and fog.

lessons.title: Normals by gradient
lessons.intro: Everything the last two modules drew came back flat, because the only question ever asked of a hit was whether it happened. Shading needs one more fact about the surface: which way it faces. Nothing in the field stores that and nothing has to. A distance field climbs away from its surface at a rate of one unit per unit, so the direction it climbs in is the direction the surface points, and that direction can be read out with nothing but subtraction. Six extra samples and one normalize, and every stage after this one has something to light.
lessons.takeaway: A distance field climbs at unit rate away from its surface, so the direction of steepest climb is the surface normal and the length of that gradient is already one — normalize is insurance rather than arithmetic. Central differences read the gradient with six extra calls to map, two per axis, and a vec2 of the epsilon and zero supplies all three offsets through swizzles rather than three more variables. The epsilon is a compromise with a floor and a ceiling: large enough that the subtraction survives float precision, small enough that both samples stay on the same piece of surface. Painting a normal is a debugging tool rather than a look, and what it paints depends on which way the camera faces — with the camera looking along positive z, a surface facing it has a normal of 0, 0, minus 1, and no blue in it whatever.
lessons.tryThis: In the second stage, work out what colour the very top of the sphere would paint if the camera could see it, then say why the render never quite gets there. In the last stage, fix the epsilon at 0.291 and predict which of the three points quoted along the row at p.y of 0.005 moves furthest from its 0.001 reading before you look.

stages.title: The slope along one axis
stages.body: map is a height above a surface, and the difference between two heights a small step apart is a slope. This stage takes one step of 0.001 either side of the hit along x, subtracts, and divides by the 0.002 the two samples are apart. The result needs no interpreting, because for an exact distance field the gradient has length one everywhere — take all three differences over 0.002 at any pixel of this disc and the vector they make has length 1.000000 in exact arithmetic. Swept over every pixel of the disc at every preview width from 240 to 560, float32 holds that to three decimals wherever the march converged, and loses it only on the outermost ring, where the march runs out of steps instead of arriving. So the single x figure already is the x component of the surface normal, and the render is that component pushed into 0 to 1 by half-plus-half. Down the vertical centre line it is 0.500000 exactly at every height, in float32 too, because a point directly ahead of the camera has no sideways tilt at all and the two samples are mirror images that cancel bit for bit; the columns half a hundredth either side of it are steady only to two decimals, reading 0.497 and 0.503 on the row at p.y of 0.005 and 0.496 and 0.504 by the top and bottom of the disc, with the row where one becomes the other landing differently in exact arithmetic than in float32. Read along the row at p.y of 0.005 on a preview an odd number of pixels across, where the columns land on whole hundredths, it climbs through 0.209, 0.291, 0.364 and 0.433 at p.x of minus 0.4, minus 0.3, minus 0.2 and minus 0.1, then 0.567, 0.636, 0.709 and 0.791 at the matching positives. An even-width preview sets its columns half a hundredth over and so never samples any of those points: either side of p.x of minus 0.4 it reads 0.204 and 0.213 instead. Three decimals is as far as a central difference on this field can honestly be taken. map is a length of about 1.0008 with 1 subtracted from it, so each sample has thrown away most of its significant digits before the two are subtracted from each other, and dividing what is left by 0.002 magnifies one float32 step at 1.0 into about three hundred-thousandths of the painted value. The steps between those readings — 0.067, 0.069, 0.073 and 0.082 going outward — are not equal, because a sphere turns away faster near its edge than near its middle. The disc is the same 0.5335 of p the march has produced since Module 8, and it sits well clear of the sides at every preview width.

stages.title: All three, and a colour
stages.body: Repeat the subtraction on y and on z, put the three differences in a vec3 and normalize. For an exact field that last step changes almost nothing, since the vector was already unit length, but it costs one operation and rescues any field that is not exact. That is normalAt, and the bill is six extra calls to map on top of everything the march already spent. Painted straight through half-plus-half, the sphere is not the pale blue this trick is usually shown producing. Dead ahead the surface faces the camera and the camera looks along positive z, so the normal on the axis is 0, 0, minus 1 and the paint is 0.500, 0.500, 0.000 — an olive with no blue in it at all. No preview samples that point exactly: the nearest row sits half a hundredth off it, and the axis is a column only where the preview is an odd number of pixels across, so the reading is 0.500, 0.503, 0.000 there and 0.497 or 0.503, 0.503, 0.000 where the two nearest columns straddle it instead. Blue only appears as the surface turns side-on: 0.020 at p.y of 0.205, 0.048 at 0.305, 0.097 at 0.405 and 0.209 at 0.505. Geometry puts a ceiling on it: at the silhouette the normal is perpendicular to the ray that grazed it, so its z component is minus a third and the paint would be 0.333. Do not go looking for that number on screen. The march paints a disc out to 0.5335 of p but converges only out to 0.5309, so the outermost 0.0026 of that radius — about a quarter of a row — is exhausted marches and nothing else: seventy-two rays along the rim of a 280, 320 or 480-pixel preview spend all sixty-four steps creeping past the tangent without ever converging, and the body counts them as hits because it only asks whether t is under 20. The worst of them, at p of minus 0.415, minus 0.335, paints 0.943 of blue where the converged pixel one column inward paints 0.273. Red and green do the travelling instead. Up the centre column green runs 0.503, 0.570, 0.639, 0.713 and 0.796 at p.y of 0.005, 0.105, 0.205, 0.305 and 0.405, and on that column green and blue shift by under 0.0002 when the sampling column moves half a hundredth, so those figures hold whichever preview reads them. Red is the channel that moves: on the whole-hundredth grid it reads 0.209 at p.x of minus 0.4 and 0.791 at plus 0.4, symmetric because the sphere is, while the even-width columns either side of minus 0.4 give 0.204 and 0.213.

stages.title: A crease in the field is a crease in the normal
stages.body: Module 9's welded pair, painted by its normal instead of filled flat. min hands back whichever sphere is nearer, so on the plane x equals zero the field stops following one and starts following the other, and every one of normalAt's six samples switches with it. The result is a seam that no amount of care in the march would smooth. At the two columns an even-width preview sets either side of the seam, p.x of minus 0.005 and plus 0.005, the colour is 0.930, 0.509, 0.245 and 0.070, 0.509, 0.245: red jumps 0.860 between two adjacent columns while green and blue do not move at all, because only the x component of the normal flips. Further out, on the whole-hundredth columns of an odd-width preview, the two lobes read as the ordinary spheres they are — 0.148, 0.509, 0.145 at p.x of 0.05, 0.232, 0.509, 0.078 at 0.1, 0.395, 0.508, 0.011 at 0.2, and 0.743, 0.509, 0.063 at 0.4; an even-width preview lands half a hundredth to one side of each and comes within 0.011 of them. The outline is Module 9's to four decimal places, a waist of 0.1220, lobes 0.2550 tall and ends at 0.4841, because nothing about the shape has changed, only what is painted on it. One pixel is worth knowing about. A preview an odd number of pixels across has a column sitting exactly on x equals zero, and there the two spheres are equidistant, so the two x samples are equal and their difference is exactly zero: that column paints 0.500, 0.519, 0.000, a value belonging to neither side of the seam.

stages.title: How far apart to sample
stages.body: The 0.001 was a decision, not a constant of nature, and here it sweeps from 0.001 to 0.291 and back every 12.57 seconds. The march is untouched — its hit threshold is still 0.001 — so the outline never moves and the only thing changing is the colour painted on it. What changes is concentrated at the seam, and it spreads in proportion. Measured along the row at p.y of 0.005, the band where the colour has moved more than 0.01 from its 0.001 reading reaches p.x of 0.0260 at an epsilon of 0.05, 0.0540 at 0.10, 0.0840 at 0.15 and 0.1155 at 0.20 — a little over half the epsilon each time, since that is roughly how far a sample has to reach to straddle the crease. At the top of the sweep it reaches 0.2155 and the seam has become a wide soft ridge. The point at p.x of 0.05, on the whole-hundredth grid again, tells the same story from the inside: 0.148, 0.509, 0.145 at the bottom of the sweep, 0.174, 0.509, 0.121 at an epsilon of 0.10, 0.332, 0.511, 0.029 at 0.20 and 0.413, 0.512, 0.008 at the top, red climbing toward the 0.500 that means no sideways tilt at all, because the two samples now sit one on each sphere and very nearly cancel. Away from the join almost nothing happens: p.x of 0.44 moves from 0.829 to 0.826 across the whole sweep and p.x of 0.30 from 0.560 to 0.553 — less, in both cases, than moving the sampling column half a hundredth to either side moves them. Too large costs you every corner in the scene. Too small costs you something the render cannot show — the two samples come to differ by less than the float can resolve, the subtraction returns noise or nothing, and normalize of a vector that is nearly zero is not defined.

lessons.title: Diffuse
lessons.intro: A normal is a direction, a light can be a direction, and dot compares two directions — which is the whole of the oldest shading model there is. What makes it convincing is not that it is accurate, because it is not, but that it has the right shape: a surface square-on to the light takes everything, a surface edge-on takes nothing, and everything between falls off as the cosine of the angle. Module 4 introduced dot as a way of projecting one vector onto another and measuring how much they agree. Here that agreement is a brightness, and the four stages are the term itself, the clamp it cannot do without, a light that moves, and the floor that stops the dark side being a hole.
lessons.takeaway: dot(n, l) is the cosine between the surface and the light, so it is one square-on, zero edge-on and negative behind. max against zero throws the negative half away, and it has to be thrown away rather than left to the display to clip, because anything added afterwards would be added to a negative. The terminator is not a threshold or a decision, it is exactly the set of points where that cosine is zero, which is why it lands in the same place however the shading around it is scaled. An ambient constant is not physics; it is an admission that the model counts one light and no bounces, and writing it as a floor plus a scaled cosine keeps the top of the range exactly where it was.
lessons.tryThis: In the second stage, work out where the terminator would move to if l became normalize(vec3(0.0, 0.0, -1.0)), and say why that answer leaves the whole visible sphere lit. Then in the last stage raise the ambient from 0.12 to 0.5, and predict what happens to the terminator's visibility — and to the top of the range — before you look.

stages.title: dot(n, l), all of it
stages.body: l is a direction, not a position: normalize(vec3(0.6, 0.7, -0.5)) is 0.57208, 0.66742, minus 0.47673, a light up and to the right and somewhat behind the camera's shoulder. Its dot with the unit normal is the cosine of the angle between them, so it runs minus one to one, and this stage paints all of it through half-plus-half rather than throwing the negative half away. At p of 0, 0.005, the nearest sample to the axis, the normal is all but 0, 0, minus 1, the cosine is 0.48117 and the pixel reads 0.741. Up the vertical centre column it climbs 0.741, 0.783, 0.822, 0.858 and 0.890 at p.y of 0.005, 0.105, 0.205, 0.305 and 0.405; downward it falls 0.736, 0.689, 0.636 and 0.574 at minus 0.005, minus 0.105, minus 0.205 and minus 0.305. Somewhere in there it passes through 0.500 exactly, which is a cosine of zero, which is the surface turned ninety degrees from the light. That is the terminator, and it is a hard fact rather than a soft one: on the centre column it falls at p.y of minus 0.399, and on the columns half a hundredth either side at minus 0.397 and minus 0.402. Along the row at p.y of 0.005 it crosses at p.x of minus 0.433. Past that line the value is genuinely negative — 0.442 at p of 0, minus 0.455 means a cosine of minus 0.115 — and a negative brightness is a number that will quietly corrupt anything it is later added to.

stages.title: max against zero
stages.body: One max, and the back of the sphere stops lying. The clamped cosine multiplies a base colour of 0.31, 0.84, 1.0, so the lit side carries the colour at whatever fraction the geometry allows and the far side is exactly black. At p of 0, 0.005 the factor is 0.4812 and the pixel is 0.149, 0.404, 0.481; at p of 0, 0.205 the factor is 0.6438 and the pixel 0.200, 0.541, 0.644; at p of 0.305, 0.305 it is 0.9278 and 0.288, 0.779, 0.928. Past the terminator everything is 0, 0, 0 — darker than the 0.05, 0.05, 0.08 background, which is the giveaway that this model has no notion of light arriving any other way. The brightest point is the one whose normal equals l exactly, and that is the world point 0.572, 0.667, 2.523. It projects to p of 0.340, 0.397, a radius of 0.523 against a silhouette of 0.5335 — so the peak of a sphere lit from over your shoulder sits within two per cent of the outline rather than anywhere near the middle, and the bright part reads as a crescent hugging the upper right rim. The clamp matters for a reason this stage cannot show. Painted on its own, a negative factor is clipped by the display and looks exactly like black; added to anything else, it subtracts from it.

stages.title: A light you can move
stages.body: l is built from iTime now: sine and cosine of an angle, scaled by 0.9 into x and y, with minus 0.5 fixed in z. Because sine squared plus cosine squared is one, the vector before normalize has the same length at every angle, so the light neither brightens nor dims as it goes round — it swings on a cone about the view axis, holding minus 0.48564 in z throughout, and returns to where it started every 12.57 seconds. The render is therefore one picture rotating, which is exactly the point: the terminator is a fixed arc that spins. At the start of the cycle the light is straight up, l is 0, 0.87416, minus 0.48564, and the terminator crosses the vertical centre column at p.y of minus 0.343, with the cosine reading 0.491 at p.y of 0.005 and 0.909 at 0.405 — two figures that do not care which preview reads them, because at this instant l has no x component and the picture is symmetric about that column, so an even-width preview's half-hundredth offset only shows up in the fifth decimal. A quarter of the way round the light points straight out to the right and the same arc has turned ninety degrees with it, crossing the row at p.y of 0.005 at p.x of minus 0.343. Half way round the light is underneath and the dark cap is on top, crossing at p.y of plus 0.343. Nothing in the shader knows where anything is in the world; each pixel compares two directions, and moving the light is nothing more than changing one of them.

stages.title: A floor under the dark
stages.body: Real dark is not black, because light arrives off everything else in the room, and the cheapest possible acknowledgement of that is a constant. Written as 0.12 plus 0.88 times the clamped cosine, the shading factor still tops out at exactly 1.0 where the normal equals l, so nothing is lost at the bright end and the whole range is simply compressed into 0.12 to 1.0. The dark side is now 0.037, 0.101, 0.120 — the base colour at twelve per cent — which is a shape you can read against the 0.05, 0.05, 0.08 background rather than a hole punched in it. It is worth noticing that it is not uniformly brighter than the background: its red is lower and only its green and blue are higher, so the dark side reads as a cool cast rather than a lift. Elsewhere the change is a straight remap. At p of 0, 0.005 the factor goes from 0.4812 to 0.5434 and the pixel from 0.149, 0.404, 0.481 to 0.168, 0.456, 0.543; at p of 0, 0.205 it goes 0.6438 to 0.6865 and 0.200, 0.541, 0.644 to 0.213, 0.577, 0.687; at p of 0, minus 0.305 it goes 0.1474 to 0.2497. The terminator has not moved by a pixel — it is still exactly where the cosine crosses zero, at p.y of minus 0.399 on the centre column — but it has stopped being an edge between shading and nothing, and that alone is most of what makes the sphere read as an object.

lessons.title: Specular
lessons.intro: Diffuse shading answers a question about the surface and the light and stops there. Move your head and nothing changes, which is right for chalk and wrong for almost everything else. A highlight is the part of the answer that depends on where you are standing. Light arrives, bounces off the surface the way a mirror would, and you see a highlight wherever that bounce happens to be aimed at your eye. That is one call to reflect, one dot against the direction back to the camera, and one exponent to say how polished the surface is — and it is the first shading term in this course that reads rd.
lessons.takeaway: reflect(-l, n) is where the light would go if the surface were a mirror, and the specular term is how nearly that direction points back at the eye. Because it involves rd it is the first term that changes when you move rather than when the object does, and its peak is not the diffuse peak: it sits where the normal bisects the light and the view. The exponent controls the width of the lobe and not its height, halving the width for every quadrupling of the exponent. And a highlight added on top of a body colour will clip on anything already bright; mixing toward the highlight colour instead keeps every channel inside 0 to 1 by construction, because both ends of the mix already are.
lessons.tryThis: In the second stage, work out what the term at the centre pixel comes to at an exponent of 3, given that it is 0.488 before the power is applied, and check it against the 0.238 the exponent of 2 produces. Then in the last stage change the 0.55 to 1.0 and say which pixel reaches pure white first, and what the render loses when it does.

stages.title: The bounced direction
stages.body: reflect takes an incoming direction and a normal and hands back the direction a mirror would send it: reflect(I, N) is I minus twice dot(N, I) times N. Since l points from the surface toward the light, the incoming ray is minus l, and since rd points from the camera into the scene, the direction back toward the eye is minus rd. The cosine between those two is what this stage paints, with nothing raised to any power yet, so what appears is a wide soft blob rather than a highlight. On the centre column — a real column only where the preview is an odd number of pixels across — it is 0.488 at p.y of 0.005, then 0.678, 0.795, 0.813 and 0.686 at 0.105, 0.205, 0.305 and 0.405, rising and then falling again, which a diffuse term never does on a convex shape. The light is off to the right, so unlike a diffuse term this one is not symmetric about that column, and the offset shows: an even-width preview reads 0.478 and 0.497 at the two columns straddling the axis. Its own columns are the ones that give the row at p.y of 0.005, where it reads 0.656, 0.744, 0.739 and 0.599 at p.x of 0.105, 0.205, 0.305 and 0.405. The peak is 1.000 and it sits at p of 0.198, 0.231, a radius of 0.304 — well inside the disc, and nowhere near the diffuse peak at 0.340, 0.397. Halving the sum of l and the view direction predicts where it ought to be: for a pixel looking straight down the axis that gives the surface point 0.333, 0.388, 2.141, which projects to p of 0.233, 0.272. The real peak sits nearer the middle than that, because every pixel has its own view direction and the one that finally satisfies the mirror condition is not the axial one.

stages.title: The exponent is the polish
stages.body: Raising a number below one to a power pushes it toward zero, and pushes it harder the further below one it already was — so an exponent narrows the blob without moving its peak. Here the exponent doubles six times over, sweeping 2 to 128 and back every 15.71 seconds, and the width halves every time it quadruples. Measured across the row at p.y of 0.235, which runs through the peak, the span where the term is at least half its maximum is 0.4406 of p at an exponent of 2, 0.2366 at 8, 0.1208 at 32 and 0.0606 at 128. The peak itself barely notices: at p of 0.195, 0.235 it reads 0.99975, 0.99899, 0.99598 and 0.98400 across those same four. Everything else collapses. At p of 0.105, 0.105 the term is 0.704 at an exponent of 2, 0.246 at 8, 0.0037 at 32 and nothing that survives four decimal places at 128; at p of 0, 0.005 it is 0.238, then 0.0032, then nothing at all. A high exponent does not make a surface brighter, it makes it more selective about which pixels see the light source at all, and a selective surface reads as a hard one.

stages.title: It follows the eye
stages.body: The camera slides sideways, 1.2 either way every 17.95 seconds, without turning: the sphere slips across the frame, its centre running from p.x of minus 0.6 at one end of the travel to plus 0.6 at the other. The diffuse term is drawn faintly underneath so there is something to judge the highlight against, and the highlight is mixed toward white on top of it. Watch which of the two stays put. The diffuse peak is the point whose normal equals l, and that is the world point 0.572, 0.667, 2.523 whatever the camera does — it is only ever seen from a new angle, projecting to p of 0.340, 0.397 from the middle of the travel and minus 0.373, 0.397 from one end. The highlight is not attached to the surface at all. At the middle of the travel it sits on the world point 0.276, 0.322, 2.093; at the far end it has slid to 0.499, 0.306, 2.189, a quarter of a unit away across the surface. On screen it moves from p of 0.198, 0.231 to minus 0.481, 0.210, which measured from the sphere's own centre is a shift from 0.198 to 0.120 — the highlight crawling toward the middle of the disc as the surface it is standing on turns. A diffuse surface looks the same from everywhere. A shiny one does not, and that is the whole of the difference.

stages.title: Adding it up
stages.body: Three terms, and the last line is deliberately not a sum. Ambient plus diffuse gives the body colour, topping out at exactly 1.0 where the normal equals l because 0.12 plus 0.88 is 1; the highlight then pulls that toward white by 0.55 of the specular term. Adding is the obvious move and it does not survive the arithmetic. At p of 0.195, 0.235 the specular term is 0.994, and the body colour plus 0.55 of it comes to 0.804, 1.243, 1.376 — of which the display can show 0.804, 1.000, 1.000, the peak flattened into a white patch with its shape gone and the falloff around it gone too. Mixing keeps every channel in range by construction, since both ends of the mix already are: the same pixel comes back 0.663, 0.862, 0.923, and the brightest channel anywhere in the frame is exactly 1.000, reached at the diffuse peak rather than inside the highlight. Away from the highlight nothing changes at all — 0.168, 0.456, 0.543 at p of 0, 0.005, 0.213, 0.577, 0.687 at p of 0, 0.205, 0.077, 0.210, 0.250 at p of 0, minus 0.305, and 0.037, 0.101, 0.120 across the whole dark side — because at an exponent of 48 the specular term is already under a ten-thousandth by p of 0.305, 0.305.

lessons.title: Soft shadows
lessons.intro: A surface that faces the light is not necessarily lit — something else may be in the way, and nothing computed so far can tell the difference. The test is another march, starting at the surface and pointing at the light: if it meets anything before it leaves, the light never arrived. That gives a shadow with a hard edge, which is the shadow a light of no size would cast. Keeping the closest the ray ever came to a surface, rather than only whether it touched one, buys the soft edge a real light casts, for the price of one min inside a loop that was running anyway.
lessons.takeaway: A shadow is a second march, from the surface toward the light, and its answer is a yes or a no unless you keep more than the answer. The smallest ratio of clearance to distance travelled is the half-angle of the widest cone the ray managed to keep clear; scaled by k and clamped it becomes a penumbra whose width halves every time k doubles, while the umbra stays exactly where the hard test put it. The start offset is not a fudge factor to be tuned by eye. Below the hit threshold divided by the cosine between surface and light every surface shadows itself, because the march that found the surface left the field under that same threshold; and above the chord a grazing ray cuts back through its own object, the shadow lets go of the thing casting it.
lessons.tryThis: In the third stage, work out the penumbra width at a k of 128 from the five figures given, and say why the umbra's edge does not move with it. In the last stage, predict which fails first as the offset climbs — the slab's cast shadow or the ball's own dark cap — and give the reason before you watch it happen.

stages.title: Marching toward the light
stages.body: The scene is a unit ball resting on a slab whose top face is the plane y equals minus one, so the two touch at exactly one point. The camera sits level with the ball's centre, which puts the slab's far edge — it stops at z of 8 — at p.y equals minus 0.1875, and the ball, which reaches 0.5336 above and below the middle, stands across that line and hides it for p.x within 0.499 either side. n.y separates the two surfaces: the slab's normal is exactly 0, 1, 0, and no ray that lands on the ball can land where n.y exceeds two root two over three — 0.9428, the value at the edge of the cap the camera can see at all, since being visible at all forces n.z below minus a third. What is tested, though, is where the march stopped rather than where a ray landed, and the grazing rays Lesson 1 caught out never landed at all. normalAt takes them regardless, and the nearest surface answers: beside the ball that is the slab, which returns 0, 1, 0 and lays a sixty-pixel thread of slab grey round the outline on a 280, 320 or 480-pixel preview; above the ball it is still the ball, and a radial normal read past the closest approach is not bound by the cap, four pixels going over it at those widths — two of them at 0.956 and two at 0.952 — and two reaching 0.985 at 371. No width between 240 and 560 puts a ball-sided pixel at 0.999, so the step holds — but on the emulator by 0.014 rather than the 0.056 the cap suggests, and it is the grid keeping it there rather than the geometry. shadow marches from the hit point toward the light, returning 0 the moment the field drops under the threshold and 1 by either of two other exits: getting 12 units out, or using up all 48 iterations unblocked. The second is not hypothetical — 85 lit pixels leave that way on the narrowest preview and on the widest alike, rays that set off nearly along the surface they left. Painted as nothing but that 0 or 1, the render is three flat regions. The ball's dark cap is its own body blocking the light, and its edge falls at p.y of minus 0.353 on the centre column. The ellipse on the slab is the ball's cast shadow: it crosses the row at p.y of minus 0.505 at p.x of minus 0.912 and plus 0.206, the row at minus 0.605 at minus 0.559 and minus 0.048, and the column at p.x of minus 0.605 between p.y of minus 0.599 and minus 0.324. There is no penumbra anywhere in it, and that is honest — this is exactly the shadow a light that is a point rather than an object casts.

stages.title: The shadow is not the terminator
stages.body: Multiplying the mask into the diffuse term puts this scene's two kinds of dark side by side, and they are not the same kind of thing at all. The terminator is where the surface turns away from the light: on the ball's centre column the cosine reaches zero at p.y of minus 0.346, and the shading fades smoothly into it. The cast shadow is where something is in the way, and it has no gradient whatever. The slab's normal never changes, so its cosine is a constant 0.67492 everywhere and its shading is flat — at p of 0.605, minus 0.505 it reads 0.389, 0.396, 0.425, and at p of minus 0.605, minus 0.505, which is the same distance from the camera at the same angle to the light and differs only in having the ball between it and the light, it reads 0.055, 0.056, 0.060, the ambient floor and nothing else. Step further out to p of minus 1.005, minus 0.505 and it is back to 0.389, 0.396, 0.425 with a step edge between. On the ball the two effects meet: 0.185, 0.502, 0.597 at p of 0, 0.205, 0.136, 0.368, 0.438 at p of 0, minus 0.005, and 0.047, 0.126, 0.150 at p of 0, minus 0.305, where the cosine has nearly run out on its own. One of these darks you could have predicted from the normal alone. The other needed a second march.

stages.title: How close it came
stages.body: The hard version throws away everything it learned on the way. At every step it holds d, the clearance where it stands, and t, how far it has come; d over t is the half-angle of the cone the ray still has clear, and the smallest such ratio over the whole march is how nearly the ray was blocked. Keeping that, scaled by k and clamped, turns the same loop into a penumbra for the price of one min. k sweeps 4 to 64 and back every 15.71 seconds and the fade narrows in exact proportion: measured along the row at p.y of minus 0.505, on the shadow's right-hand edge, the span between a factor of 0.95 and one of 0.05 is 0.0746 of p at a k of 4, 0.0358 at 8, 0.0178 at 16, 0.0086 at 32 and 0.0040 at 64 — halving for every doubling, which is what dividing an angle by k means. The umbra does not move while that happens. The 0.05 crossing sits at p.x of 0.2090, 0.2070, 0.2060, 0.2058 and 0.2058 across those five, against the hard shadow's edge at 0.2060, so k buys the width of the fade and never the size of the shape. At the loose end the fade carries a long way: at a k of 4 the point at p of minus 1.005, minus 0.505 is down to 0.256 of full light, where at 16 it is untouched at 1.000.

stages.title: Where the shadow ray starts
stages.body: The shadow march has to start somewhere, and the one place it cannot start is where it already is. The main march stops when the field falls under 0.001, so at the hit point the field is under 0.001 by definition — a shadow ray beginning at a t of zero samples that same point, finds it under the threshold and reports the surface as blocking itself. Every pixel whose march converged goes black; the only survivors are the grazing threads at the ball's rim and along the horizon whose march ran out of steps and never reached a surface at all. Climbing out of that takes a start larger than the threshold divided by the cosine between the surface and the light. On the slab that cosine is 0.67492, so 0.001 over 0.67492, which is 0.001482, is enough, and this sweep spends just under six-tenths of every 15.71-second cycle below it. On the ball the requirement grows without limit as the surface turns toward the terminator, which is why the speckle clears from the middle outward and survives longest exactly where the shading was about to go dark anyway. Too large is the opposite failure and it is much quieter. The slab's shadow edge barely notices: between a start of 0.002 and one of 0.45 the crossing on the column at p.x of minus 0.605 moves from p.y of minus 0.5988 to minus 0.5992, four ten-thousandths, because out there the shadow ray has more than a unit of clear space before it reaches the ball and skipping the first half of a unit changes nothing. What does move is the ball's own edge. It retreats from p.y of minus 0.348 at a start of 0.02 to minus 0.353 at 0.05, minus 0.392 at 0.15, minus 0.435 at 0.30 and minus 0.470 at 0.45 — because a ray leaving a point just past the terminator cuts a chord back through the ball twice as long as that cosine, and a start longer than the chord steps straight over it. The true terminator is at minus 0.346, and every one of those readings is already past it.

lessons.title: Fog
lessons.intro: Distance is the one thing a march always knows and the one thing shading has so far never used. Fog spends it. Mix the shaded colour toward a fog colour by an amount that grows with t, and two things happen at once: near objects separate from far ones in a way no amount of lighting achieves on its own, and the place where the scene runs out stops being a visible edge. The second is the practical one. Every finite scene has a far plane somewhere, and fog is how you stop drawing attention to it — provided the fog colour is what is behind the far plane already.
lessons.takeaway: Fog is one mix, and the only real decision is what the factor does with t. One minus e to the minus t times a density ties the near field and the far field together, so any density strong enough to hide a far plane also drains the foreground; squaring t before the exponent separates them, because the factor then grows slowly near the camera and very fast further out. None of it hides anything unless the fog colour is what the background already is, which in practice means taking the sky's horizon colour and using the same constant in both places. And the far plane has not moved — fog does not trim the scene, it removes the contrast that made the edge of it visible.
lessons.tryThis: In the third stage, work out the density that would put the far edge at exactly 99 per cent fog on the centre line, given that t there is 8.062, and compare it with the 0.07 the stage uses. Then swap that stage's fog colour for the sky's upper colour and say which part of the horizon shows the mismatch most strongly, and why it is that part rather than the other.

stages.title: Distance into a mix
stages.body: The scene is the last lesson's, shaded with an ambient floor, a clamped cosine and a soft shadow at a k of 16, and then mixed toward a pale grey-blue by a factor that grows with depth. One minus e to the minus t times a density is the standard shape: zero at the camera, approaching one without ever arriving, and with nothing to tune but the density. At 0.18 the nose of the ball, at a t of 2.0, is already 30.2 per cent fogged. The slab directly under it at p of 0, minus 0.905 is nearer, at a t of 1.934, and 29.4 per cent; the slab at p of 0, minus 0.605 is further, at 2.671, and 38.2 per cent; the far edge of the slab, at 8.062 on the centre line, is 76.6 per cent. The depth ordering of the ground is worth pausing on: the bottom row of the frame is the nearest ground and it recedes as you go up, so the fog on the slab increases upward, not downward. The trouble is at both ends at once. The ball is washed out when it should be crisp, and the far edge is still a quarter of the way from the fog colour, so the hard line where the slab stops is as visible as ever against the dark background behind it.

stages.title: What hiding the far edge costs
stages.body: The density sweeps 0.02 to 0.60 and back every 17.95 seconds, and there are two numbers to watch: the far edge of the slab, at a t of 8.062 on the centre line, and the nose of the ball at 2.0. At a density of 0.02 they are 14.9 and 3.9 per cent — the far edge is a hard line and the ball is clean. At 0.1 they are 55.3 and 18.1. At 0.2, 80.1 and 33.0. At 0.3, 91.1 and 45.1. At 0.45, 97.3 and 59.3. At 0.6, 99.2 and 69.9. Hiding a far edge properly wants better than 99 per cent, and by the time the density is high enough for that, the ball has lost seven-tenths of itself. That is not a tuning problem you can win with a better number, it is the shape of the function: e to the minus t times density falls at a rate proportional to how much is left, which is the same proportion everywhere, so one constant controls the near field and the far field together and there is no setting at which one is crisp and the other is gone.

stages.title: Square the distance, and match the sky
stages.body: Two changes at once, because neither works without the other. Squaring t before the exponent unties the near field from the far one: the factor now grows slowly at first and then very fast, so the foreground keeps its contrast while the far field saturates outright. At a density of 0.07 the ball's nose at a t of 2.0 is 24.4 per cent fogged — less than the 30.2 the plain version managed at 0.18 — while the far edge of the slab at 8.062 is 98.94 per cent, against that version's 76.6. Saturating is only half the job, though, because fog hides a far plane only if what lies beyond the far plane is already the fog colour. So the background is now a sky built from rd.y whose pale end is the same 0.62, 0.70, 0.80 the fog mixes toward. smoothstep from 0 to 0.6 gives every ray pointing at or below the horizontal that horizon colour exactly — the whole lower half of the frame — and above it the sky darkens with rd.y. Not evenly across a row, though. rd.y is p.y over the length of p.x, p.y and 1.5, so a pixel out to the side has a longer denominator and a flatter ray, and the sky brightens toward the sides: on the top row rd.y is 0.553 on the centre column, 0.437 at the side edge of the narrowest preview and 0.332 at the side edge of the widest. Read up the centre column, where the ball's outline reaches 0.5336 and the slab fills every row below the ball, so the first row of real sky is the one at p.y of 0.535: the sky is 0.368, 0.509, 0.705 at p.y of 0.605, 0.296, 0.455, 0.677 at 0.795 and 0.257, 0.425, 0.662 on the top row. Read across that top row instead and the same three channels come back 0.317, 0.471, 0.685 at the narrowest preview's side edge and 0.405, 0.538, 0.719 at the widest's — 15 and 38 levels of 255 of red above what the middle of the frame shows. What is left of the seam is small enough to measure. The last row that lands on the slab is p.y equals minus 0.195; the row above it, at minus 0.185, would meet the plane at z of 8.11 and so passes over the far edge and shows sky. On that last row, either side of the ball at p.x of plus or minus 0.605 — a column that three of the four common previews have and the odd-width one does not — the slab comes back 0.61827, 0.69771, 0.79717 against a sky of 0.62000, 0.70000, 0.80000: a difference of 0.0028, or 0.72 of a level out of 255, and 0.73 and 0.71 at the columns half a hundredth either side that the odd-width preview reads instead. At every width it rounds to one level rather than to none. At p.x of plus or minus one it is 0.0009, under a quarter of a level, and further out there is nothing left to measure, because the slab's far edge is further away there: 8.062 on the centre line, 9.667 at p.x of one, and 10.99 and 15.13 out at the side edges of the narrowest and the widest previews. The slab still ends at z of 8, where p.y is minus 0.1875. Nothing has been trimmed. The edge has simply stopped having any contrast to be seen by.

stages.title: The finished thing
stages.body: Everything the module built, in one shader: a normal from six extra samples of the field, an ambient floor with a clamped cosine on top, a soft shadow folded into the diffuse term and into the highlight both, so a shadowed surface has no highlight either, the highlight mixed toward white rather than added, and fog over the lot against a sky the fog matches. Nothing clips anywhere. The brightest channel in the frame is 0.918, at p of 0.358, 0.384, inside the ball's highlight. The ball reads 0.299, 0.558, 0.656 at p of 0, 0.205 and 0.484, 0.721, 0.813 at p of 0.205, 0.205. The ground reads 0.426, 0.461, 0.513 at p of 0, minus 0.605 and 0.516, 0.563, 0.631 at p of 0.605, minus 0.505, while the shadowed point at the mirror position, p of minus 0.605, minus 0.505, comes back 0.368, 0.412, 0.469 — a shadow you can still see the ground through rather than a hole in it. That last figure is the fog earning its keep a second time. Mixing toward a light colour by distance hides the far edge and lifts the shadows at the same time, because the two are the same operation, and there is nothing left in this frame that a flat fill and a hit test could have told you.
